case_studies.title: Separating Thinking from Spelling for Efficient Generative Recommendation
case_studies.abstract: Generative recommenders retrieve items by writing their semantic IDs (SIDs) code by code under trie-constrained beam search, an approach now deployed on large web platforms. Standard autoregressive interfaces pay for the SID length K twice: a history of T items enters the backbone as TK code tokens, and every beam-search step runs through the backbone, so returning B candidates costs O(BK) backbone decode tokens per user. The second cost often dominates, and it grows with the backbone, the SID depth and the candidate budget. We introduce Deco (decoding from concepts), which separates reading t
case_studies.summary: Deco cuts the compute needed to generate recommendation candidates by separating the semantic ID lookup from the heavy decoding step, reducing the number of backbone token passes from O(BK) to a smaller, more efficient operation. The research built a prototype system that achieves faster beam‑search for recommendations while maintaining quality, showing measurable speed‑ups and cost reductions on large‑scale web platforms. For a typical cloud infra manager, this means lower compute usage and faster response times for recommendation services.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage recommendation workloads, 1) evaluate whether your current model uses beam‑search that scans full semantic IDs; 2) switch to a Deco‑style pipeline that decouples ID look‑up from backbone decoding; 3) monitor CPU/GPU utilisation and latency – you should see a drop in decoding token count and faster candidate generation.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes an optimization for generative recommenders that could reduce compute cost on recommendation systems deployed at scale, relevant for IT engineers managing cloud and SaaS infrastructure. However, it appears to be a research prototype with no released code or production deployment, so maturity is moderate. Monetisation potential is modest: engineers could implement the technique to lower inference costs, but it would require significant engineering effort and is not an out‑of‑the‑box product.

case_studies.title: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search
case_studies.abstract: Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD. LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a
case_studies.summary: The research tackles two problems with low‑rank SVD compression of large language models: it improves how ranks are assigned to each layer and fixes the rank collapse caused by traditional Fisher estimators. By adding a layer‑wise error model (LEMS) and a new KFAC‑SVD method, the authors achieve better accuracy‑cost trade‑offs than previous techniques. The result is a more efficient, accurate compressed model that uses fewer compute resources.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for LLM deployments, 1) evaluate whether your current compression pipeline uses global rank allocation; 2) implement the LEMS layer‑wise error estimator to adjust rank per layer; 3) integrate KFAC‑SVD to avoid rank collapse and test the model’s inference cost on your existing GPU clusters.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a method for compressing LLMs, which could reduce compute costs for on-premises or cloud deployments—relevant to IT engineers managing AI workloads. However, the work appears theoretical with no evidence of an open-source implementation or production deployment, limiting immediate usability. The approach is potentially monetisable by reducing inference costs, but the path to a commercial product is not fully defined, so the score is modest.

case_studies.title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox
case_studies.abstract: Personal email agents decide, for every message, what it is, whether it is urgent, whether to draft a reply, create a task, or ignore it. Their error rate is rarely measured: the stored labels were written by the system itself. We present Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent in daily use, and a measurement protocol (stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, pre-registered hypotheses, human labels in the agent's review loop) that yields ground truth before any training. case_studies.summary: This research builds a self‑hosted personal email assistant called Foyer and introduces a rigorous way to measure its decisions before training, showing how to get accurate ground truth labels for email routing tasks. It solves the problem of unreliable error rates in personal inbox agents by providing a practical protocol for labelling emails. The study ran on 739 real Italian/English emails and produced a reliable measurement framework.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a personal email agent and a measurement protocol, which might interest IT engineers who manage personal productivity tools. However, it is niche, not directly affecting infrastructure or large-scale automation, and lacks clear deployment or commercial applicability within 90 days. The system is likely still in experimental stages with limited released code. Therefore scores are low across all criteria.

case_studies.title: Monetizing Intelligence: Advertising and Subscription Design on LLM Platforms
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) platforms introducing advertising must decide how much capability ad revenue should fund and what consumers should pay to avoid ads. We study a monopolistic platform that jointly chooses costly response quality, advertising intensity, and subscription prices when advertising reduces user value but better service raises advertising returns. Three findings follow. First, when partly ad-supported and ad-free plans coexist, advertising can finance useful service for consumers who receive none under pure subscription. case_studies.summary: This research tackles how an LLM platform can balance advertising revenue, subscription pricing, and service quality to maximise value. The authors built a model that jointly sets ad intensity, response quality, and subscription fees, showing that ad‑supported plans can fund better service for users who otherwise pay nothing. The findings are mainly theoretical and specific to platform business models, not directly relevant to day‑to‑day IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper discusses pricing strategy for ad-supported LLM services; limited direct relevance to IT infrastructure operations. No evidence of deployed system or code, and monetisation model is theoretical rather than immediately actionable for engineers.

case_studies.title: Green Code or Costly Code? Evaluating the Energy Costs of Iterative LLM-Based Code Optimizations
case_studies.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to optimize code for performance. This practice often assumes that improvements in execution speed naturally translate into overall lower energy consumption. We challenge this assumption empirically by measuring whether performance-optimized code produced by LLM self-refinement pipelines is also energy-efficient relative to canonical human reference solutions, and whether the energy cost of the optimization process can be offset by subsequent execution-time savings. We evaluate 11 open-source models across four decoding configurations on all 1
case_studies.summary: The study shows that using LLMs to auto‑optimize code can raise the overall energy bill, even if the resulting code runs faster. Researchers built a self‑refinement pipeline, tested 11 models on a set of tasks, and found that the extra compute cost of the optimisation often outweighs the runtime savings. This matters to cloud managers because it flags a potential hidden cost when deploying LLM‑based optimisation tools.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If your org uses LLM‑based code optimisation, immediately measure the energy cost of the optimisation pipeline versus the runtime savings of the final code. Compare the energy per run with the baseline; if the optimisation cost is higher, consider disabling or throttling the feature.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses energy costs of LLM-driven code optimisation, which could inform IT engineers' decisions about code performance vs. energy consumption. However, it remains an academic study without a ready-to-deploy system or clear commercial product, limiting immediate applicability and monetisation potential.
